8.title: Reverse Mortgages Explained: How They Actually Work (and Who They're Really For)
8.metaDescription: A plain-English breakdown of how reverse mortgages work, what they cost, and when tapping home equity in retirement actually makes sense.
8.bodyHtml:
A reverse mortgage lets homeowners 62 and older convert home equity into cash without selling the house or taking on a monthly payment. It's the opposite of a regular mortgage: instead of your balance shrinking every month, it grows. For the right person, it can be a legitimate retirement tool. For the wrong person, it can quietly eat through the biggest asset they own. Here's how it actually works, what it costs, and how to tell which camp you're in.

What a Reverse Mortgage Actually Is

The vast majority of reverse mortgages are Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs), which are insured by the Federal Housing Administration. A HECM is the FHA-insured reverse mortgage for homeowners 62+. Rather than making payments to a lender, the lender makes payments to you, drawn from your home's equity. While HECM borrowers must continue paying critical property charges, like taxes and insurance, they're not required to make monthly principal and interest mortgage payments.

Borrowers can defer repayment of the loan balance to a much later date — typically until they pass away or permanently move out of the home. During that time, interest and fees keep getting added to the balance, which is why the loan grows instead of shrinks.

Who Actually Qualifies

Eligibility isn't just about turning 62. Lenders look at several things:

  • Age: You must be at least 62 for a home equity conversion mortgage (HECM) loan.
  • Residence: The home must be your primary residence, and eligible property types include single-family homes, HUD-approved condos, 2-4 unit properties where you occupy one unit, and certain manufactured homes.
  • Counseling: HECM borrowers must complete counseling through a U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)-certified counseling agency. Sessions cost $145 to $200, take about an hour, and end with a certificate valid for 180 days.
  • Financial assessment: The HECM Financial Assessment is a mandatory underwriting procedure required by the FHA for every reverse mortgage applicant nationwide, evaluating your willingness and ability to meet all ongoing financial obligations associated with homeownership. If you don't pass, the lender may require a Life Expectancy Set-Aside — money held back from your proceeds specifically to cover future property taxes and insurance.
  • No delinquent federal debt: HUD does not allow delinquent federal debt.

How Much You Can Actually Borrow

The amount you qualify for depends mainly on your age, current interest rates, and your home's value — up to a federal cap. The Federal Housing Administration increased the maximum claim amount for Home Equity Conversion Mortgages in calendar year 2026 from $1,209,750 to $1,249,125, effective for case numbers assigned on or after January 1, 2026. If your home is worth more than that, a home valued at $1,300,000 would have its lending value capped at the limit — the extra value simply doesn't count toward your loan.

Even within that cap, you don't get to borrow the full value. Borrowers typically receive 30%–60% of their home's value, with loan size affected by home value, interest rates, existing mortgage balances, and payout type. Older borrowers generally qualify for a higher percentage than younger ones, because the loan is expected to run for fewer years.

There's also a first-year limit. The 60% rule refers to the initial disbursement limit that HUD has in place, limiting a reverse mortgage borrower to advance 60% of the Principal Limit at the time of closing and during the first year of the loan being in place. There's an exception when the existing mortgage needing to be paid off exceeds that threshold — in that case, you can pay it off and receive an additional 10% of the Principal Limit.

Three Ways to Get the Money

You're not locked into one style of payout:

  • Lump sum: All eligible funds at closing, subject to the 60% rule. Interest starts accruing on the full amount immediately.
  • Monthly payments: Either for a fixed term or for as long as you live in the home (tenure).
  • Line of credit: The most flexible option, and the one most borrowers choose. Interest accrues only on the amount borrowed, not on the unused portion of the credit line. Any unused portion of the credit line may grow over time, with the growth rate tied to the loan's adjustable interest rate plus the annual Mortgage Insurance Premium. The available line of credit cannot be frozen, reduced, or canceled simply because home values decline — a real difference from a HELOC, which can be frozen or cut if your home's value drops or you miss payments.

What It Actually Costs

This is where a lot of the sales pitches get vague. The real cost structure looks like this:

CostAmount
Upfront mortgage insurance premium2% of the home's value or the FHA limit, whichever is less
Annual mortgage insurance premium0.5% of the outstanding balance, charged for the life of the loan
Origination feeCapped by HUD at $6,000
Closing costs (appraisal, title, counseling, etc.)Typically $10,000–$15,000 total, often financed into the loan

For HECMs originated after 2017, mortgage insurance premiums are broken into an initial premium of 2% due at closing and an annual mortgage insurance premium equal to 0.5% of your outstanding mortgage balance. The loan origination fee equals either $2,500 or 2% of the first $200,000 of your home's appraised value, whichever is greater, plus 1% of your home's value above $200,000, capped at $6,000. Most of these fees get rolled into the loan rather than paid out of pocket, which sounds convenient but means they're quietly reducing the equity you have left.

What Happens to the House Later

This is the part people underestimate. The loan becomes due when the last borrower dies, sells, or moves out permanently — and there's a real clock once that happens. Once heirs receive a due and payable notice from the lender, they have 30 days to buy, sell, or turn the home over to the lender to satisfy the debt. It might be possible for the timeline to be extended up to six months so heirs can sell the home or obtain their own loan to purchase it. If they aren't able to sell the home or secure financing within six months, they can apply for up to two 90-day extensions.

The good news is that the loan is non-recourse. A reverse mortgage is a non-recourse loan, which means that if the loan balance exceeds the home's value when it's sold, heirs aren't responsible for the difference — the insurance premium homeowners pay ensures this protection. But it also means any equity you were hoping to leave behind shrinks every year the loan is outstanding.

Reverse Mortgage vs. HELOC

FeatureReverse Mortgage (HECM)HELOC
Monthly paymentsNot requiredRequired
Age requirement62 or olderNone
Credit line can be frozen/reducedNo, as long as loan terms are metYes, if values drop or payments are missed
Upfront costsHigher (insurance premiums, origination fee)Typically lower
Balance over timeGrowsShrinks as you pay it down

Proprietary reverse mortgages and HELOCs can be frozen if values drop or payments are missed. That's a meaningful advantage for a reverse mortgage if your goal is a guaranteed source of funds you can't have pulled out from under you — but it comes at a real price in fees and lost equity.

Does It Affect Social Security or Medicaid?

Reverse mortgage proceeds are considered a loan, not income, so funds are not taxable and do not affect Social Security or Medicare benefits. The exception is needs-based programs. Reverse mortgage proceeds do not affect Social Security benefits but can affect needs-based programs such as Medicaid. If you're on or expect to need Medicaid or SSI, talk to your counselor about how a lump sum could push you over asset limits before you take one.

The Scam Risk Is Real

Reverse mortgages are a frequent target for fraud aimed at seniors. Reverse mortgages are complex loans, making them the perfect breeding ground for a scam, and unfortunately scammers use this type of loan to take advantage of older Americans, stealing their hard-earned money and, in some cases, their homes. Common red flags include unsolicited offers, pressure to sign quickly, and anyone claiming to offer a "VA reverse mortgage" — the Department of Veterans Affairs does not offer reverse mortgage loans, so anyone selling one specifically for veterans is running a scam. The HUD-required counseling session exists specifically to put a neutral third party between you and the sales pitch — don't skip it or treat it as a formality.
